heuristics.rule: Negotiate before signing, not after onboarding
heuristics.condition: When you have received a written offer but have not yet signed or started
heuristics.action: Raise all compensation concerns — salary, equity, level, benefits — before you sign, because this is the only window where your negotiating position is equal to the employer's
heuristics.because: Multiple commenters agree: once you join, you lose leverage entirely — you are on the boat, the boatman sets the price. The offer stage is legally a non-binding offer (要约) and no contract has formed yet.

heuristics.rule: Use competing offers or a walkable current job as leverage before negotiating
heuristics.condition: When you want to negotiate upward on a received offer
heuristics.action: Establish real alternatives first — other offers, a viable current job — then name your number directly without embarrassment
heuristics.because: Commenter with 100% and 50% salary jump experience attributes both outcomes to consistently declining below-expectation offers until the right one came; leverage is what makes the ask credible

heuristics.rule: Acknowledge the offer warmly, then open the negotiation with specific market data
heuristics.condition: When negotiating compensation after receiving a written offer
heuristics.action: Call or email HR: thank them, reaffirm interest, then cite market benchmarks and concrete benefit comparisons to justify the ask
heuristics.because: Commenter describes this exact script from US business school career office training and personal experience in both China and the US

heuristics.rule: Total compensation includes non-salary items that can be monetized — negotiate on all of them
heuristics.condition: When the base salary is hard to move
heuristics.action: Calculate the value of paid leave, bonus structure, equity, welfare benefits, and paid holidays and use them as comparison points or negotiation targets
heuristics.because: Commenter explicitly lists 14–15 month salary, extra PTO, full social insurance, holiday gifts, annual trips as items that can be 折成金钱 (converted to monetary value) in negotiation

decision_factors.factor: Whether you are a fresh graduate (应届生) or an experienced professional
decision_factors.why_it_matters: Fresh graduates have significantly less bargaining power due to no track record and no competing offers; negotiation strategy differs substantially
decision_factors.how_to_assess: Count years of work experience; if zero, treat as low-leverage scenario and focus on any unique strengths rather than market comps

decision_factors.factor: Whether you have real, walkable alternatives
decision_factors.why_it_matters: Without alternatives, a negotiation ask has no credible threat; the employer knows you will likely accept anyway
decision_factors.how_to_assess: Do you have another offer in hand, or a current job you are genuinely fine staying at? If not, your leverage is low

decision_factors.factor: How critical the role is to fill (岗位稀缺性)
decision_factors.why_it_matters: If the position has been open a long time and good candidates are scarce, the hiring manager has incentive to go back to leadership to re-approve a higher package
decision_factors.how_to_assess: Research how long the job posting has been up; ask during interview how urgently they need to fill it; note whether the recruiter is following up urgently

decision_factors.factor: Whether the negotiation requires the hiring manager to re-open internal approval flow
decision_factors.why_it_matters: In many companies, offer approval involves the manager's own leadership; re-opening it costs the manager political capital and signals poor interview execution, making them resistant
decision_factors.how_to_assess: Ask HR directly whether the compensation is flexible or fixed by band; large companies typically have rigid bands, smaller companies have more discretion

hidden_tradeoffs.choice: Accepting an unsatisfactory offer without negotiating, planning to 'prove yourself' and ask for more after joining
hidden_tradeoffs.unstated_consequence: Salary adjustments in large companies are tied to fixed review windows; you cannot negotiate outside those windows, and by the time the window opens you are already bound by the contract you signed
hidden_tradeoffs.who_it_affects: New hires at large tech companies or corporations with formal HR cycles (most US and Canadian big tech)

hidden_tradeoffs.choice: Joining at a salary you are unhappy with and trying to leave shortly after
hidden_tradeoffs.unstated_consequence: Short tenure is interpreted as either performance failure or poor decision-making by future employers; you also bear switching costs — relocation, gap in bonus/vesting, re-onboarding time
hidden_tradeoffs.who_it_affects: Candidates who rationalized the low offer as temporary and did not negotiate at the offer stage

hidden_tradeoffs.choice: Not negotiating because you 'don't want to cause trouble' for the hiring manager
hidden_tradeoffs.unstated_consequence: You absorb all the cost of the manager's internal process, while the manager and company retain the full benefit of your labor at below-market rate
hidden_tradeoffs.who_it_affects: Risk-averse candidates, international students, and fresh graduates who fear rejection

failure_patterns.pattern: Accepting the offer and planning to renegotiate after a successful probation period
failure_patterns.why_it_happens: Candidates feel grateful or anxious about losing the offer; they rationalize that proving themselves first will make the ask easier and safer
failure_patterns.consequence: The labor contract locks in the salary; HR has no budget or process mechanism to adjust outside review cycles; the informal promise from the recruiter is unenforceable
warning_signs: Candidate says 'I'll just show them what I can do first'
Recruiter makes a vague verbal promise about 'adjusting after probation' instead of putting it in the offer letter

failure_patterns.pattern: Raising compensation concerns only after onboarding, once fully committed
failure_patterns.why_it_happens: The candidate felt the offer stage was too early or too risky to push back; they hoped their dissatisfaction would fade
failure_patterns.consequence: No leverage remains — switching costs (housing, visa, social insurance timelines) make leaving expensive; the company has little incentive to re-negotiate a signed contract
warning_signs: Candidate says 'I'll bring it up once I've proven myself'
Candidate mutters dissatisfaction but signs without saying anything

failure_patterns.pattern: Negotiating with no market data and no competing offer — just a vague sense that 'I deserve more'
failure_patterns.why_it_happens: Candidate knows negotiation is allowed but has not done the preparation to make a credible case
failure_patterns.consequence: HR has nothing to take back to leadership; the ask sounds arbitrary and is easily dismissed; candidate may still accept the same offer, having gained nothing
warning_signs: Candidate says 'I just feel the number is low' without citing comparables
No other offer or current salary benchmark to reference

diagnostic_questions.question: Do you have a competing offer or a current job you are genuinely fine staying at?
diagnostic_questions.what_it_reveals: Whether the candidate has real leverage to negotiate or is negotiating from desperation
diagnostic_questions.follow_up_if_yes: Use the competing offer or current comp as your anchor — name the specific number and ask them to match or exceed it
diagnostic_questions.follow_up_if_no: Focus on market data (Glassdoor, Levels.fyi, LinkedIn Salary) and unique qualifications as your justification; the ask is weaker but still worth making

diagnostic_questions.question: Are you a fresh graduate (应届生) or do you have work experience?
diagnostic_questions.what_it_reveals: Whether market-rate comps and job-offer leverage arguments apply, or whether the candidate is in a fundamentally lower-leverage position
diagnostic_questions.follow_up_if_yes: Experienced hire: negotiate assertively using market benchmarks and competing offers
diagnostic_questions.follow_up_if_no: Fresh graduate: still negotiate, but anchor on any differentiating strengths (special skills, research, internship outcomes) rather than pure market comps

diagnostic_questions.question: Has the offer been signed/accepted, or are you still in the pre-signature window?
diagnostic_questions.what_it_reveals: Whether negotiation is still at the optimal moment or whether it requires re-opening a closed contract
diagnostic_questions.follow_up_if_yes: Pre-signature: this is legally the best moment — no binding contract exists yet; negotiate now
diagnostic_questions.follow_up_if_no: Post-signature: leverage is severely diminished; wait for the formal salary review window and prepare a strong business case

industry_realities.common_belief: You should not negotiate after receiving an offer because it will make you look difficult and the company will rescind the offer
industry_realities.actual_reality: HR's KPI is to hire the right person within budget — losing a good candidate over a small salary gap is worse for them than adjusting the number. Informed commenters from both China and US contexts agree: negotiating at the offer stage is expected, especially for experienced hires
industry_realities.implication: Candidates should negotiate without guilt; the fear of rescission is almost always unfounded for reasonable asks backed by market data

industry_realities.common_belief: You can negotiate a salary adjustment after probation by making an informal agreement with the recruiter or manager
industry_realities.actual_reality: Large companies have rigid salary adjustment windows (typically annual or semi-annual reviews) and the labor contract already specifies the salary; informal pre-hire verbal promises are legally unenforceable and HR departments cannot act on them outside the formal cycle
industry_realities.implication: Never trade away the offer-stage negotiation for a vague post-probation promise; get any adjustment commitment in writing in the offer letter or do not accept it as a real commitment

industry_realities.common_belief: Asking for more money after receiving an offer means the manager has to embarrass themselves by going back to their boss
industry_realities.actual_reality: True in some rigid hierarchies, but this is the candidate's problem being described from the manager's perspective — it is not the candidate's responsibility to protect the manager's face at the cost of their own compensation
industry_realities.implication: The manager's internal approval burden is real, but it is their job to handle; a well-prepared, market-anchored ask is a legitimate business request, not a personal attack on the manager

junior_vs_senior_signals.naive_pattern: First-timer waits until after joining to raise salary concerns, believing they need to 'earn the right' to ask first
junior_vs_senior_signals.informed_pattern: Experienced professional negotiates before signing because they know that is the only moment of equal power; once inside the boat, the power balance flips permanently
junior_vs_senior_signals.why_it_matters: Post-onboarding negotiation is nearly impossible in structured companies; the window closes the moment you sign

junior_vs_senior_signals.naive_pattern: Accepts silently to avoid seeming difficult, suppresses dissatisfaction, and hopes it fades
junior_vs_senior_signals.informed_pattern: Treats the dissatisfaction as a signal that must be surfaced and resolved before signing, because unresolved dissatisfaction will create ongoing distraction, ongoing job searches, and eventual turnover
junior_vs_senior_signals.why_it_matters: Suppressed dissatisfaction does not fade — it festers and leads to low engagement or premature departure, which costs both sides more than the salary gap would have

junior_vs_senior_signals.naive_pattern: Sees asking for more money as confrontational, risky, and likely to offend the hiring manager or HR
junior_vs_senior_signals.informed_pattern: Sees it as a normal bilateral process — the offer is a non-binding proposal (要约), you have not accepted yet, expressing counter-terms is legally and professionally standard
junior_vs_senior_signals.why_it_matters: The framing determines whether they act at all; treating it as confrontation leads to paralysis and acceptance of under-market pay

community_misconceptions.misconception: Once you receive an offer, negotiating will almost certainly cause the company to rescind it or view you as a troublemaker
community_misconceptions.why_believed: The top answer on this post describes the manager's internal re-approval burden and the risk of being labeled a '刺头' (troublemaker), making the risk feel very concrete and personal
community_misconceptions.actual_rule: Negotiation at the offer stage is standard practice and expected by HR; the cost of losing a good candidate over a modest salary gap is higher than the cost of adjusting the number. Multiple informed commenters with real hiring experience explicitly contradict the 'rescission risk' framing
community_misconceptions.real_consequence: Candidates who believe this misconception silently accept below-market offers, leading to ongoing dissatisfaction, distraction, and eventual turnover — outcomes worse for both parties than the negotiation would have been

community_misconceptions.misconception: If you negotiate and the salary can't be raised now, you can agree with the recruiter to get a raise after a successful probation period
community_misconceptions.why_believed: It feels like a reasonable compromise — prove yourself first, then get rewarded. Recruiters sometimes make this vague promise to close the hire
community_misconceptions.actual_rule: Labor contracts lock in salary on signing; large companies have formal salary review cycles and cannot make ad-hoc adjustments outside them; informal verbal promises from recruiters are unenforceable and HR management will not honor them because it creates untracked budget variance
community_misconceptions.real_consequence: The candidate signs at a salary they are unhappy with, the informal promise is never honored, and they have no recourse — the optimal negotiation window has passed

real_case_outcomes.situation: Experienced professional in Shanghai receiving job offers below salary expectations during two separate job changes
real_case_outcomes.decision: Consistently declined all offers where HR or headhunters said the compensation could not meet the stated expectation, without exception
real_case_outcomes.outcome: First job change resulted in a 100% salary increase; second resulted in a 50% increase
real_case_outcomes.lesson: Credible walkaway behavior — actually declining non-matching offers rather than capitulating — is what produces large compensation gains; the willingness to walk is the leverage, not the negotiation script

real_case_outcomes.situation: Candidate received an offer where salary had not been explicitly negotiated during interviews — only a rough range was discussed — in both a Chinese company and a US company
real_case_outcomes.decision: Proactively called/emailed HR after receiving the written offer: thanked them, reaffirmed interest, then explicitly raised compensation concerns with market data and benefit comparisons
real_case_outcomes.outcome: The negotiation was treated as normal by HR in both cases; the process described as standard by the US business school career office as well
real_case_outcomes.lesson: The written offer is the correct and expected trigger point for compensation negotiation; doing it by phone or email with a warm, professional framing and market-based justification is standard practice in both markets

psychological_barriers.trigger: Candidate asks 'will negotiating hurt my chances or make them think badly of me?' after already receiving an offer
psychological_barriers.underlying_state: Fear of rejection and loss aversion — the offer feels like a fragile gift that could be taken away; asking for more feels like threatening the relationship
psychological_barriers.how_it_manifests: Candidate accepts the first number without speaking, or asks tentatively and backs down immediately at any resistance
psychological_barriers.expert_move: Reframe: the offer is a non-binding proposal (要约), not a favor or a contract. You have made no commitment yet. Expressing counter-terms is the legally and professionally expected next step, not an act of ingratitude. HR's job is to close you within budget — they are on your side of this.

psychological_barriers.trigger: Candidate says 'I'll just show them what I can do first, then ask for more after probation'
psychological_barriers.underlying_state: Sunk cost pre-commitment combined with hope bias — believing future performance will create a negotiation opportunity that doesn't structurally exist
psychological_barriers.how_it_manifests: Candidate signs a below-market offer, joins the company, discovers salary review windows are rigid and informal promises evaporate, and is stuck for 12+ months
psychological_barriers.expert_move: Ask directly: 'Can you show me where in the employment contract the post-probation adjustment is documented?' If it is not in writing in the offer letter, it does not exist. The negotiation window is now, not later.

psychological_barriers.trigger: Fresh graduate (应届生) who feels they have no leverage and treats any salary as 'take it or leave it'
psychological_barriers.underlying_state: Status anxiety and imposter syndrome — believing their inexperience disqualifies them from having preferences or making asks
psychological_barriers.how_it_manifests: Accepts first offer without any negotiation, sometimes even expressing gratitude for a below-market number
psychological_barriers.expert_move: Even fresh graduates have negotiable dimensions: start date flexibility, signing bonus, professional development budget, equity cliff timing. The ask does not have to be base salary. Negotiating one dimension builds the muscle and sometimes opens the door to others.

reframing_moves.original_framing: Can I still negotiate after receiving an offer, or is it too late / too risky?
reframing_moves.reframe: This is not the last chance to ask — it is the ONLY chance. Once you sign and join, you are on the boat and the boatman sets the terms. The offer stage is the single moment when you and the employer have roughly equal power.
reframing_moves.why_it_works: Shifts the question from 'is it acceptable to ask?' to 'if not now, when?' — which reveals that waiting is not a safer option but actually the highest-risk move
reframing_moves.example_language: 见过艄公行船到江心敲乘船的竹杠，可没见过乘船的到了江心问艄公讨自己船票钱的 (You've seen the boatman raise prices at midstream — you've never seen a passenger demand a refund at midstream)

reframing_moves.original_framing: I don't want to seem greedy or cause problems for the hiring manager by asking for more
reframing_moves.reframe: Meeting recruiter targets within budget is the HR's KPI — not yours. Your job is to represent your own interests. The candidate who silently accepts a bad deal and then underperforms or leaves in 6 months is far more costly to the company than the candidate who negotiated up front.
reframing_moves.why_it_works: Depersonalizes the negotiation — it reframes it as two professionals doing their respective jobs, removing the guilt and the feeling of imposing on someone
reframing_moves.example_language: 你的利益，自己不捍卫，别人犯得着多发你钱吗？(Your interests — if you don't defend them yourself, why would anyone else pay you more?)

reframing_moves.original_framing: I'm not happy with the salary but I'll accept and prove myself, then ask for a raise after probation
reframing_moves.reframe: The satisfaction you expect to feel after 'proving yourself' will not arrive — it will be replaced by the same dissatisfaction, now with additional switching costs making it harder to leave. Unresolved dissatisfaction does not fade; it festers.
reframing_moves.why_it_works: Forces the candidate to think about the trajectory of accepting, not just the immediate relief of avoiding a difficult conversation
reframing_moves.example_language: 一旦有某些点触动到你，心里会更加难受 (Once something triggers you, the feeling only gets worse — it doesn't fade)
